## Setup

```{python}
import pandas as pd

url = 'https://eds-217-essential-python.github.io/data/national_parks.csv'
parks = pd.read_csv(url)
parks.shape
```

```{python}
parks.columns.tolist()
```

## Part 1: Filtering

**1. How many rows describe units whose `unit_type` is exactly `National Park`?**

```{python}
national_parks = parks[parks['unit_type'] == 'National Park']
national_parks.shape
```

```{python}
national_parks['unit_name'].nunique()
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**4,743 rows, but only 61 National Parks.** A row is one park in one year, not one park, and the
file covers 113 years of records. If you wrote "there are 4,743 National Parks" you read the row
count as a count of things in the world, which it is not.

`National Park` is also only one of 30 values in `unit_type`. Most of the file is National
Monuments, Historic Sites and the rest of the National Park Service, so this filter throws away
about four fifths of the table.
:::

**2. How many rows have a `year` of `Total`? Use `~` or `!=` to build a table called `by_year`
that has none of them in it. How many rows does `by_year` have?**

```{python}
totals = parks[parks['year'] == 'Total']
print(totals.shape)

by_year = parks[~(parks['year'] == 'Total')]
print(by_year.shape)
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**386 `Total` rows, leaving 21,174 rows in `by_year`.** The number 386 is not arbitrary: it is
exactly the number of distinct units in the file, so every unit carries one and only one `Total`
row.

Those rows are sums of the other rows in the same table. Great Smoky Mountains has a `Total` of
521,947,058, and adding up its 113 yearly values gives 521,947,058 as well. Leaving them in means
counting every visitor twice, once in the year they visited and once in the lifetime sum. Every
ranking in Parts 2 and 3 depends on having removed them first.
:::

**3. The `region` column uses two-letter codes. Build a list of the codes `PW`, `IM`, and `AK`,
and use `.isin()` to filter `by_year` down to units in those three regions. How many rows?**

```{python}
western_regions = ['PW', 'IM', 'AK']
western = by_year[by_year['region'].isin(western_regions)]
western.shape
```

```{python}
by_year['region'].value_counts()
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**9,894 rows, which is 46.7% of `by_year`.** Three of the eight region codes hold almost half the
records, and `IM` on its own is the largest region at 5,682 rows. That is a fact about where the
Park Service has units, not about where people go.

`.isin()` with a list does the work of three separate comparisons joined by `|`. The list is the
part you edit later, which is why building it as a named variable is worth the extra line.
:::

**4. Using two conditions in one filter, find the rows that are National Parks and recorded more
than 5 million visitors. How many are there, and what does each row represent?**

```{python}
big = by_year[(by_year['unit_type'] == 'National Park') & (by_year['visitors'] > 5_000_000)]
print(big.shape)
big[['year', 'unit_name', 'state', 'visitors']].sort_values('visitors', ascending=False).head()
```

```{python}
big['unit_name'].value_counts()
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**59 rows, and each one is a single park in a single year.** So the honest sentence is "there
were 59 park-years above 5 million visitors", not "59 parks passed 5 million".

The distinction matters because only **four** parks ever did it. Great Smoky Mountains accounts
for 55 of the 59 rows, Grand Canyon for two (2015 and 2016), Yosemite for one (2016) and Acadia
for one (1989). A row count of 59 sounds like a broad group and is in fact one park repeated.

Acadia's single appearance is worth a second look. It recorded 5,440,952 visitors in 1989,
4,502,283 in 1988, and then 2,339,591 in 1990. A 57% drop in one year almost certainly reflects a
change in how the Park Service counted visitors rather than a real change in visits. Keep that in mind
before treating any single year as a fact about the world.
:::

## Part 2: Ranking

**5. Rank all of `parks` by `visitors`, largest first, and look at the top 10. Something is wrong
with this answer. Say what, and say why in one sentence.**

```{python}
parks.sort_values('visitors', ascending=False).head(10)[
    ['year', 'unit_name', 'unit_type', 'visitors']
]
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**Every one of the top 10 is a `Total` row.** Sorting the unfiltered table compares 113-year lifetime
sums against single years, and a lifetime sum is always the larger number. The largest value,
Blue Ridge Parkway at 871,922,828, is not a number of visitors in any year at all.

Notice what the wrong answer looks like. There is no error message. The output is a clean,
well-formatted table built from the wrong rows. Nothing in the output tells you the rows are not
comparable. You have to know that from having looked at the `year` column.
:::

**6. Fix it, and rank `by_year` instead. Which single park unit had the highest visitor count in
any one year, and in what year?**

```{python}
by_year.sort_values('visitors', ascending=False).head(10)[
    ['year', 'unit_name', 'unit_type', 'state', 'visitors']
]
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**Golden Gate National Recreation Area, in 1987, with 21,767,176 visitors.**

The part worth arguing about with your partner is that it is not a National Park. The whole top
10 is Golden Gate National Recreation Area and Blue Ridge Parkway, and no National Park appears
anywhere in it. The question asked about park *units*, and units include parkways, recreation
areas and memorials, most of which are free, urban, and easy to drive through.

If you answered "Great Smoky Mountains", you answered a different and narrower question. That is
not a small slip. It is the same ambiguity question 12 asks you to name.
:::

**7. Filter to National Parks in the year `2016`, then find the top 10 by visitors. Show only the
`unit_name`, `state`, and `visitors` columns.**

```{python}
np_2016 = by_year[(by_year['unit_type'] == 'National Park') & (by_year['year'] == '2016')].copy()
print(np_2016.shape)

np_2016.sort_values('visitors', ascending=False).head(10)[['unit_name', 'state', 'visitors']]
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**61 National Parks reported a 2016 figure, and Great Smoky Mountains leads with 11,312,786
visitors, close to twice the second-place Grand Canyon at 5,969,811.** After that the list
descends gently: Yosemite 5,028,868, Rocky Mountain 4,517,585, Zion 4,295,127, and on down to
Glacier at 2,946,681.

The shape of the ranking matters more than its order. These ten parks account for 57.5 percent of
all 83,920,334 National Park visits in 2016, so the distribution is heavily concentrated at the
top and has a long thin tail. Note also that this is a different table from question 6, where no
National Park appeared at all.
:::

**8. How many of the 61 National Parks recorded more than a million visitors in 2016?**

```{python}
(np_2016['visitors'] > 1_000_000).sum()
```

```{python}
print(np_2016['visitors'].sum())
print(np_2016[np_2016['visitors'] > 1_000_000]['visitors'].sum() / np_2016['visitors'].sum())
print(np_2016['visitors'].median())
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**22 of the 61, so just over a third.** Those 22 parks account for 81.4% of the 83,920,334 visits
recorded to National Parks in 2016, which is the more useful way to say it: a third of the parks
receive four fifths of the visits.

The other 39 are much smaller than the top 10 table suggests. The median park recorded 607,479
visitors, and the smallest, Gates of the Arctic in Alaska, recorded 10,047. Any sentence that
begins "national parks are crowded" is really a sentence about roughly twenty of them.

Note that `(np_2016['visitors'] > 1_000_000).sum()` counts `True` values rather than adding
visitors. Summing a boolean Series is the standard way to count matches without building a second
table.
:::

**9. Use `.idxmax()` and `.loc[]` on `np_2016` to print the name of the most-visited National Park
of 2016 on its own, without displaying the whole row.**

```{python}
busiest = np_2016['visitors'].idxmax()
print(np_2016.loc[busiest, 'unit_name'])
print(np_2016.loc[busiest, 'visitors'])
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**Great Smoky Mountains National Park, with 11,312,786 visitors**, which is 1.9 times Grand
Canyon's 5,969,811 and 13.5% of all National Park visits that year. The gap between first and
second place is larger than second place itself.

`.idxmax()` returned the index **label** of the largest row, not the value. That is exactly why it
is paired with `.loc[]`: one step answers "which one?" and the next answers "how much?", and
neither step requires you to look at a table with your eyes.
:::

## Part 3: Put them together

**10. Build a list of the state codes `CA`, `UT`, and `AZ`. Filter `np_2016` to National Parks in
those three states, rank them by visitors, and display the whole ranked list.**

```{python}
southwest_states = ['CA', 'UT', 'AZ']
southwest = np_2016[np_2016['state'].isin(southwest_states)].copy()

southwest.sort_values('visitors', ascending=False)[['unit_name', 'state', 'visitors']]
```

**11. Which of those three states has the park at the top of your list, and which has the most
parks in it? Answer both in a markdown cell. You can count the parks per state by eye from your
ranked table.**

```{python}
southwest['state'].value_counts()
```

```{python}
{state: southwest[southwest['state'] == state]['visitors'].sum() for state in southwest_states}
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**Arizona has the top park; California has the most parks.** Grand Canyon leads the list with
5,969,811 visitors, and Arizona has only three National Parks in total. California has nine, more
than Utah's five and Arizona's three, and its best park, Yosemite at 5,028,868, is second.

The two questions have different answers, and that is the reason both were asked. Arizona reaches
7,433,511 visits in 2016 with three parks, four fifths of them at one park. California reaches
12,345,331 with nine, of which five recorded under 610,000 apiece. "Which state has the busiest
park" and "which state has the most park visiting" and "which state has the most parks" are three
different questions, and a single ranked table answers none of them by itself.

These 17 parks are 28% of the 61 National Parks and 35.6% of 2016 National Park visits.
:::

**12. In one markdown cell of three or four sentences, answer this: a colleague asks you which
national park is "the busiest". What do you need to know before you can answer, and what would you
tell them? Use at least two numbers from today's work.**

```{python}
y2016 = by_year[by_year['year'] == '2016']
y2016.sort_values('visitors', ascending=False).head(5)[
    ['unit_name', 'unit_type', 'state', 'visitors']
]
```

There is no single right answer here. A strong response names at least two of the three choices
that have to be settled before the question means anything, quotes at least two numbers it
actually computed, and gives the colleague a usable answer rather than only an objection. Here is
one that would earn full marks.

:::{.callout-note title="✅ A model answer"}
Before I can answer I need three things settled. First, which units count: only the 61 National
Parks, or all 386 National Park Service units? Second, which year, or whether they mean the
all-time total. Third, whether the `Total` rows have been removed, because leaving them in makes
every answer a lifetime sum.

If they mean National Parks in 2016, the answer is Great Smoky Mountains with 11,312,786 visitors,
nearly twice Grand Canyon's 5,969,811. If they mean all Park Service units in 2016, Great Smoky
Mountains is third: Golden Gate National Recreation Area recorded 15,638,777 and Blue Ridge
Parkway 15,175,578. If they mean the busiest single year ever recorded, it is Golden Gate in 1987
at 21,767,176.

So the answer I would give is: for National Parks, Great Smoky Mountains, and the margin is large. But
if they are asking because they want to know where the crowds are, the parkways and recreation
areas beat every National Park, and I would want to know what they are planning to do with the
number before I picked one.
:::

## Where the marks are

If you compare your notebook against this key, look for these four things before you look at
anything else.

1. **Your `by_year` has 21,174 rows, and you built it before you ranked anything.** Every wrong
   answer in Part 2 traces back to the 386 `Total` rows.
2. **Your answer to question 6 names a unit that is not a National Park.** Golden Gate National
   Recreation Area in 1987 is the correct answer. If you wrote a National Park, you filtered when
   the question did not ask you to.
3. **You compared `year` to the string `'2016'`, with quotes.** The column is text. Comparing it
   to the integer `2016` returns zero rows and raises no error, which makes it one of the hardest
   mistakes in pandas to notice.
4. **Your answers say what a row is.** 4,743 rows is not 4,743 parks, and 59 rows above 5 million
   is four parks, not 59. Every count in this file is a count of park-years until you say
   otherwise.
